# Job 4: research notes

**Before you use these:** I found no relevant material from Lutheran, Pentecostal/AG, Orthodox, bibleodyssey.org or catholic.com sources, so none of those appear below. The disagreements here mostly don't follow denominational lines. They come down to two questions: where Eliphaz's vision came from (vv. 12–16), and what "angels charged with error" means (v. 18). The Catholic material is two brief notes, Haydock's commentary and the Catholic Encyclopedia, both on v. 18.

---

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Whole chapter.** The NET notes divide the speech into three parts. In 4:1–11 Eliphaz wonders that Job who had comforted so many people in trouble, and who was so pious, should fall into such despair, forgetting the great truth that the righteous never perish under affliction. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Wesley's summary: Eliphaz grants that Job was once useful but concludes from his present state that he is a hypocrite. By all this he aims to make Job both penitent and patient under his sufferings. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/

**v. 1:** Teman, a region linked to Edom and famed for wisdom (Genesis 36:11; Jeremiah 49:7; Obad 8). His counsel contains some true observations about God's justice, yet his central explanation of Job's affliction will prove inadequate and will later be rebuked by the Lord (Job 42:7). https://biblehub.com/job/4-1.htm
- Guzik: Eliphaz had earned the right to speak, since in a remarkable display of friendship, he sat wordless with Job through a whole week. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-4/

**v. 2:** Wesley: He speaks with great modesty. He will not undertake the cause alone, but joins his friends with him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Eliphaz feels he has no choice but to speak, because Job has called God's wisdom and justice into question and they must be defended. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- NET notes that the speech has a distinctly Aramaic coloring to it. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm

**vv. 3–4:** NET: the Hebrew verb for "instructed" can mean either teaching or discipline. The "feeble hands" are literally hands "hanging down," a sign of weakness or despair, and the knees are pictured buckling under a heavy load (compare Heb 12:12). https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Pulpit calls these verses strong evidence of Job's kindness and practical sympathy for sufferers when he was prosperous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html

**v. 5:** Pulpit hears sarcasm here, a hardness that Job could not have missed. Its lesson: a friend's rebuke should be given with great delicacy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- Guzik quotes Andersen: "Already there is insinuation that Job is unable to apply to himself what he preached to others." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-4/

**v. 6:** Readers split on the tone (see the second section). Pulpit: if Job really is as sure of his innocence as he says, he should still trust God and expect to be delivered. If he doesn't, the obvious conclusion is that he isn't so sure after all. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- NET: "fear" means Job's reverent devotion to God. Rowley says that, coming from Eliphaz, it almost means "your religion." https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm

**v. 7:** Guzik calls this the heart of the argument: Job must be guilty of some sin, because the innocent don't suffer the way he has. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-4/
- Pulpit asks whether Eliphaz had never heard of "righteous Abel." It says the idea of "secret sins" was invented to explain why the righteous suffer, and that Eliphaz is hinting this is Job's case. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- Wesley's paraphrase of Eliphaz: Therefore thou art guilty of some great, though secret crimes, and thy sin hath now found thee out. https://ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Job.html

**v. 8:** Pulpit cross-references Prov 22:8, Hos 8:7, Hos 10:13 and Gal 6:7–8. It says Eliphaz turns a general rule into a law without exceptions, and unlike the psalmist (Ps 73:3) has never been troubled by the prosperity of the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- NET: "plowing" pictures deliberately preparing one's life for evil. It describes people who are wicked at the root. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm

**v. 9:** NET: in Gen 2:7 God's breath gives life, but here it takes life away. The Greek Old Testament (LXX) has "word" or "command" instead of "breath," perhaps to tone down the human picture of God. NET adds that the idea that misfortune always means God's anger is not necessarily the case, as the NT declares (see Luke 13:1-5). (That last quote comes from the full notes page I read.) https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Wesley: by God's hidden but mighty judgment the wicked are blown away like chaff. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm

**vv. 10–11:** Wesley: the lions stand for powerful tyrants. He adds that possibly he may secretly accuse Job, or his children, that being persons of great wealth and power, they had abused it to ruin their neighbours, and therefore were justly cut off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm
- Pulpit: Eliphaz is darkly hinting that the early deaths of Job's children may have resulted from Job's own wrongdoing. It lists five kinds of lion in these verses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- NET, citing Clines: it is probably impossible to tell the different lion words apart. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm

**v. 12:** NET: the Hebrew says the word was literally "stolen" to him, meaning it came stealthily. "Whisper" occurs only here and in Job 26:14, and the point is that Eliphaz caught just a bit of it. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Wesley: before Scripture was written, visions were God's usual way of making his mind known. He adds: How little a portion is heard of God! How little do we know of him in this world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm

**v. 13:** Pulpit: the word for "deep sleep" is the one used in Gen 2:21, Gen 15:12 and 1 Sam 26:12, and it suggests something close to a trance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- Wesley: Eliphaz was not actually asleep, since visions came to people awake, unlike dreams. https://ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Job.html

**v. 14:** Pulpit compares the "horror of great darkness" that fell on Abraham (Gen 15:12): human nature shrinks from direct contact with the spiritual world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html

**v. 15:** NET: the Hebrew *ruach* can mean "spirit" or "breath," and the commentators are divided on whether this is an apparition, a spirit, or a breath. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Pulpit disagrees with the "breath" reading: a breath of air can't "stand still" or have a "form." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html

**v. 16:** Peake: "silence and a voice" is one idea expressed with two words, meaning "a still voice." The Hebrew switches to the present tense, as if Eliphaz were living through the moment again. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-4.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the word for "form" is the most ethereal word for form, the one used in Num 12:8. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-13.html

**v. 17:** NET argues against reading "more righteous than God." It prefers "righteous before God": He is stating that no man is righteous before God. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Wesley: anyone who finds fault with God's law, grace or providence makes himself out to be more just and pure than God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm
- Bible Hub cross-references Rom 3:23. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/4.htm

**v. 18:** NET: the "servants" must be angels, given the parallel line; the Targum took them to be prophets. The word for "error" occurs only here. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Pulpit: even the highest angels fall infinitely short of God's perfection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- Readers split on whether these are fallen angels (see the second section).

**v. 19:** NET: "houses of clay" are human bodies (Job 10:9; 2 Cor 4:7 "earthen vessel"), built on dust and returning to dust. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- Wesley: immortal spirits live in mortal bodies, which are heavy burdens and traps to them. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/

**v. 20:** Wesley: there is not a moment wherein man is not sinking towards death and corruption. Perish - In reference to this present worldly life. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/
- Pulpit is also unsure that "forever" means more than disappearing from this life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html

**v. 21:** Pulpit: the "tent-cord" stands for the soul, and it "goes away" rather than perishing. People die "without wisdom" because they never learned what their trials were meant to teach them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html
- Wesley's closing comment: instead of quarrelling with his afflictions, let him admire that he is out of hell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the spirit's words end at v. 21. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-18.html

---

## Where interpreters really differ

**v. 6, the tone.** Wesley (Methodist) reads it harshly: Job's present behaviour shows his piety was but mere talk and appearance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-4.html
- NET reads it kindly: Eliphaz is not being sarcastic to Job. He knows that Job is a God-fearing man. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm

**vv. 12–16, where the vision came from.** This is the biggest disagreement.
- **From God, through a good angel.** Matthew Henry calls the spirit one of the good angels and holds the vision was real. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-13.html
  - Wesley (Methodist) says it was an angel in visible form. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/
  - Gill (labelled Calvinist on StudyLight) rejects the view that it was invented or demonic, saying this has no foundation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-12.html
- **Not from God.** Constable: his vision was not a revelation from God for the following reasons. He did not say that it was from the Lord. He adds that perhaps the spirit was an evil angel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-15.html
  - GotQuestions (evangelical) goes further: It is certain that the spirit that appeared to Eliphaz was a demon. Its reason is that holy angels came in the light and said "do not fear," while this spirit frightened Eliphaz and hid in darkness. https://www.gotquestions.org/holy-angels.html
- **Undecided.** Guzik quotes Clarke: "Whether it came from heaven or hell, we know not". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-4/
  - Pulpit's homilist Adeney: a vision proves nothing by itself, and Eliphaz's mistake was trying to overawe and silence Job by the recital of his vision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-4.html

**v. 18, which angels.**
- **The fallen angels.** Wesley: Without all doubt, this refers to those angels who foolishly and wickedly fell from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/4.htm
  - Guzik connects the verse to Satan, the real cause of Job's trouble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-4/
- **Angels are imperfect only compared with God.** Gill rejects the fallen-angel reading: "folly" is too weak a word for their rebellion. He says the verse means angels are foolish compared with God, and that God upholds them in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-18.html
  - Geneva Study Bible (Calvinist): God finds imperfection in angels when they are not maintained by his power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/4-18.htm
- **Not reliable at all.** Coffman refuses to grant any rightness whatever in this speech of Eliphaz. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-18.html

---

## Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **v. 15:** NET, citing Clines, leans toward "wind." The same verb is used of a gale in Isa 21:1, and a gust like that may be what made Eliphaz's hair stand on end. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- **v. 17:** NET argues that Eliphaz had the vision before he heard of Job's trouble, so it was not aimed at Job claiming to be more righteous than God. https://bible.org/netbible/job4_notes.htm
- **vv. 17–19:** Peake (older critical scholarship) says this text does not yet divide angels into good and bad; all are fallible. It also notes that the spirit that appears to Eliphaz knows nothing of the Fall as an explanation of human sin. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-4.html
  - Coffman disputes the claim that this contradicts New Testament teaching on angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-15.html

**Catholic readings (v. 18)**
- Haydock reads the angels as those who fell, as the fathers explain it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/4-18.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says that in Job 4:18, we seem to find a definite declaration of the fall: "In His angels He found wickedness." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01476d.htm

**Prosperity teaching (vv. 7–8, 12–16)**
- Guzik warns against treating sowing and reaping (Gal 6:7) as an absolute spiritual law. He says Paul did not promote some law of spiritual karma, which, if it existed, would condemn us all. (That quote is from the full page I read.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-4/
- John Brown (on Blue Letter Bible) compares health-and-wealth teachers directly to Eliphaz. He says they claim divine authority for "the same lie": that sickness or poverty must be the result of sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/brown_john/Job/Job_04-05.cfm
